title: Integrated rate laws & half-life
examples: How do I figure out the time for a reaction to reach half its starting amount?
What is the difference between zero order and first order reactions?
Does the initial concentration affect the half-life?

explain.say: Today we explore how reaction rates change over time.
A zero order reaction rate is constant regardless of concentration.
For a first order reaction, the rate is directly proportional to the concentration.
The half-life is the time needed for the reactant to reduce by half.
In a first order reaction, the half-life is independent of the initial concentration.
If a reaction is zero order, doubling the initial concentration halves the half-life.

faq.q: What does 'order' mean in reaction kinetics?
faq.a: The order tells you how the reaction rate depends on the concentration of reactants. A first order reaction means the rate is proportional to the concentration.
asks: How do I determine the reaction order?
What does the exponent in the rate law mean?

faq.q: Is the half-life always the same for a given reaction?
faq.a: No, the half-life depends on the reaction order. For first order reactions, it is constant, but for zero order, it changes with concentration.
asks: Does initial concentration matter for t1/2?
Is half-life constant for all reactions?

faq.q: If I know the rate constant k, can I find the half-life?
faq.a: Yes, you can use the appropriate formula based on the reaction order. Remember to check if the reaction is first or zero order.
asks: What formula uses k and t1/2?
How do I calculate half-life from k?

faq.q: What is the relationship between the rate law and the stoichiometry?
faq.a: The rate law does not always match the coefficients in the balanced chemical equation. It must be determined experimentally.
asks: Does the equation predict the rate?
Is the rate law always the same as the balanced equation?

faq.q: Can I use the integrated rate laws for any reaction?
faq.a: No, you must first determine the reaction order experimentally. Using the wrong integrated law will give incorrect results.
asks: Which law do I use for a reaction?
How do I check my reaction order?

facts: Zero order reactions have a rate law that is independent of concentration.
First order reactions have a rate law directly proportional to the reactant concentration.
For a first order reaction, the half-life is constant at a fixed temperature.
The half-life for a zero order reaction depends on the initial concentration.
